issues.legal_issue: A temporary territorial distinction in agricultural-income taxation is consistent with equality when it addresses tax-liability differences arising from the distinct legal histories of the territories and is rationally connected to bringing their taxpayers into line.
material_facts: After territorial reorganisation, different agricultural-income tax laws continued in the two parts of the newly formed State.
A court ruling meant that agricultural income in the newly added territory could not be taxed for the relevant assessment year, while comparable income in the other territory remained taxable.
The legislature enacted a temporary measure to tax income from the newly added territory, including income accruing after it became part of the State.
issues.conclusion: The territorial classification was based on an intelligible differentia with a rational connection to the object of imposing tax on the newly added territory, and did not violate equality.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution permits reasonable classification where it rests on an intelligible differentia and bears a rational relation to the legislation’s object. The classification must be assessed by the law’s real effect, not merely its wording. Tax legislation receives wider legislative latitude because of the complexity of fiscal adjustment, but remains subject to the fundamental requirements of classification. The Court applied Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, Purshottam Govindji Halai v. Shree B. M. Desai, and Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala; it also held that a territorial classification may be made by legislation enacted after a merger, with its validity assessed in light of the historical circumstances and the law’s object.

rule.if: constitutional_tax_challenge and historical_tax_liability_difference and remedial_territorial_classification and rational_connection_to_tax_object

predicates.constitutional_tax_challenge: A person challenges the constitutionality of a tax measure on equality grounds.
predicates.historical_tax_liability_difference: Different legal histories left taxpayers in the territories with different tax liabilities for the relevant period.
predicates.remedial_territorial_classification: The legislature treats the territories differently to address the tax-liability gap created by those historical circumstances.
predicates.rational_connection_to_tax_object: The territorial distinction advances the measure’s objective of imposing the intended tax liability.

issues.definition: When an equality challenge concerns a tax measure, a historically grounded territorial distinction that addresses differing tax liabilities and is rationally connected to the tax objective is treated as constitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A temporary method of deriving an average annual income to determine tax rates is not invalid merely because another method might be more favourable or precise, if the chosen method is not capricious, fanciful, arbitrary, or clearly unjust.
material_facts: The measure defined a longer previous year for taxpayers in the newly added territory and used a proportion of total income from that period to derive average annual income for applying the rate schedule and exemption limit.
Taxpayers could elect a shorter period ending on a date to which their accounts had been made up.
The measure applied the same rate structure, with rates varying by annual-income slabs, and was intended as a temporary response to the transition between different tax regimes.

The evidence did not establish that the relevant crops throughout the territory were all harvested in the short period relied on by the challengers; the Court found that the method could cause incidental advantages or hardship.
issues.conclusion: The chosen method for determining average annual income was not arbitrary or unreasonable and did not violate equality.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 applies to taxation laws, but courts do not meticulously compare the burden on every taxpayer or invalidate a legislative choice merely because another assessment method seems preferable. Where several methods are available, the chosen method is invalid only if it is capricious, fanciful, arbitrary, or clearly unjust. Incidental hardship or advantage is not sufficient where the measure operates uniformly, and its temporary transitional purpose is relevant to assessing reasonableness. The Court applied the classification principles in Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar and referred to Purshottam Govindji Halai v. Shree B. M. Desai and Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala on equality in taxation.

rule.if: constitutional_tax_challenge and tax_rate_assessment_method and temporary_transition_measure and uniform_rate_structure and method_not_capricious

predicates.constitutional_tax_challenge: A person challenges a tax measure on equality grounds.
predicates.tax_rate_assessment_method: The challenged measure derives an annual-income figure from income earned over a nonstandard assessment period to determine the applicable tax rate.
predicates.temporary_transition_measure: The measure is temporary and addresses a tax problem created by a transition between legal regimes.
predicates.uniform_rate_structure: The same rate structure applies to taxpayers covered by the measure, with rates varying according to the income figure used.
predicates.method_not_capricious: The chosen calculation method is not capricious, fanciful, arbitrary, or clearly unjust, even if it may cause incidental hardship or another method might be preferable.

issues.definition: A tax-rate calculation method survives an equality challenge when it is used in a temporary transition measure, applies a uniform rate structure, and is not capricious.

issues.legal_issue: Different practical effects within a territorially defined taxpayer class do not amount to unjust discrimination when the measure applies uniformly and the differences arise incidentally from variations in crop timing.
material_facts: The measure applied to taxpayers throughout the newly added territory and imposed the same tax treatment on them.

Evidence showed that crop-harvesting seasons varied, but most crops were harvested during similar periods across the territory; the asserted difference principally concerned one crop in part of the territory.
The resulting differences in taxpayers’ income timing were not shown to result from taxpayers being singled out for different treatment.
issues.conclusion: The differences in crop timing did not establish unjust discrimination between taxpayers within the class covered by the measure.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a law’s real effect is decisive, but equality and uniformity within a class are not defeated by advantages or disadvantages arising incidentally from a peculiar situation, so long as persons are not singled out for special treatment. This principle applies to taxation laws, subject to the requirements of reasonable classification. The Court relied on Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, Purshottam Govindji Halai v. Shree B. M. Desai, and Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala.

rule.if: constitutional_tax_challenge and uniform_treatment_within_tax_class and practical_difference_from_crop_timing and no_individuals_singled_out

predicates.constitutional_tax_challenge: A person challenges a tax measure on equality grounds.
predicates.uniform_treatment_within_tax_class: The measure gives taxpayers in the relevant class the same legal treatment.
predicates.practical_difference_from_crop_timing: Taxpayers experience different practical effects because their crops are harvested at different times.
predicates.no_individuals_singled_out: The measure does not select particular taxpayers within the class for special treatment.

issues.definition: When taxpayers in a class receive uniform legal treatment, differences caused by crop timing are not unjust discrimination if no individuals are singled out.
